newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN CMB, RAILWAYS INVEST IN ZEEBRUGGE.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN CMB, RAILWAYS INVEST IN ZEEBRUGGE.

text.p: Belgian national railways company SNCB/NMBS and shipping company CMB NV plan to make the Belgian port of Zeebrugge Europe's fastest growing container port, SNCB managing director Etienne Schouppe said on Tuesday.

"Our programme for 1997 and 1998 foresees additional investment of half a billion Belgian francs, at the end of which we want an up-to-date terminal of a capacity of about 450,000 containers per year," Schouppe told Reuters in an interview after the annual general meeting of SNCB/NMBS's Ferry-Boats shipping unit.

Ferry-Boats, which is held 83 percent by SNCB/NMBS and 9.6 percent by CMB, set up at the end of 1996 a 50/50 European Economic Interest Grouping (EEIG) with CMB unit Hessenatie to manage the two groups' interests in Zeebrugge.
An EEIG is a company whose assets remain owned by its parent shareholders.

Schouppe said the EEIG company, Ocean Container Terminal Terminal Hessenatie Zeebrugge (OCHZ), can presently handle around 180,000 containers a year. "We want to more than double the capacity," Schouppe, who is also Ferry Boats chairman, said.
Rival Belgian Antwerp port handled 29.5 million tonnes of containerised goods in 1996, or nearly 1.9 million containers or 2.65 million TEUs (Twenty foot equivalent units).
Dutch Rotterdam port, Europe's largest, handled 53.4 million tonnes.

"For the moment, Zeebrugge is the small brother of Antwerp ...but the increase that can be realised in Zeebrugge will be greater than other ports in the Le Havre (France)-Hamburg (Germany) range," Schouppe added.

The money being spent over the next two years, which comes on top of half a billion francs invested in 1996, is to be used to enlarge the terminal's infrastructure. 1996's investment was paid for partly from a capital increase at Ferry Boats which cut CMB's interest in the company to 9.6 from 13 percent.
"We want a berth of 1,000 metres which is able to serve three mega-carriers at the same time," Schouppe said.

"This (EEIG) allows to respond better to the challenge laid down a few years ago by the major shipping lines, which are reducing the number of sailings by employing bigger vessels," CMB said in its 1996 annual report.
"Hessenatie has clearly made a choice between the complimentarity of Zeebrugge and Antwerp and ended a year of expansion in the coastal port," it said.

Schouppe said he expected container vessels up to 5,000 TEU and bulk cargo traffic to continue using Antwerp port, but because of problems in dredging the Schelde river, which provides access from the sea to Antwerp, deeper, ocean-going container vessels would opt for Zeebrugge.

The growing container traffic at Zeebrugge helped Ferry Boats to a profit of 170 million Belgian francs in 1996 after it lost nearly 85 million francs in 1995. Turnover reached 1.7 billion Belgian francs, Schouppe said.
